item.title: Ankle & Foot — Muscle Energy Application
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Ankle & Foot and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: dorsiflexion/plantarflexion, foot mobility, gait, balance and load tolerance.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Supine, prone, long sitting or weight-bearing according to the technique.
Keep the foot supported and relaxed unless movement is required.
therapistPosition: Stand at the foot end or beside the ankle with the lower leg stabilized.
stabilization: Stabilize distal tibia/fibula, calcaneus or adjacent foot segment based on the target.
contact: Use broad contact over talus/calcaneus/midfoot or soft tissue and avoid excessive pressure over superficial neurovascular structures.
Position the target muscle/joint at a comfortable barrier and provide matched resistance without allowing unwanted movement.
forceDirection: Use a gentle isometric contraction, commonly about 10–30% effort, followed by relaxation and taking up the newly available range.
dosage: Usually 3–5 cycles of 5–10 second contractions before reassessment.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Ankle & Foot: dorsiflexion/plantarflexion, foot mobility, gait, balance and load tolerance.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Screen fracture, syndesmotic instability, severe swelling, neurovascular compromise and suspected DVT.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Ankle & Foot assessment → correct regional setup → Muscle Energy Application → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Soleus — MET
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve dorsiflexion with the knee flexed when soleus restriction is clinically relevant.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine, long sitting or half-kneeling with the knee flexed. Bring the ankle into dorsiflexion to the first comfortable barrier while controlling the foot.
subTechniques.contact: Stabilize the distal tibia and calcaneus/forefoot.
subTechniques.direction: Ask the patient to gently plantarflex against resistance. Relax, then move into the new dorsiflexion barrier while keeping the knee flexed.
subTechniques.reassess: Weight-bearing lunge with knee flexed, squat depth and ankle dorsiflexion.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Knee flexion reduces gastrocnemius influence, making the test/treatment more soleus-focused.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid if there is acute calf injury, marked swelling or DVT concern.

subTechniques.name: Peroneal / Fibularis Group — MET
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve selected inversion/adduction restriction or lateral-leg guarding when the fibularis group is clinically relevant.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Long sitting with the foot supported. Move gently toward inversion/adduction only to the first comfortable barrier.
subTechniques.contact: Stabilize the distal leg and control the lateral forefoot.
subTechniques.direction: Ask the patient to gently evert the foot against resistance. Relax, then take up the new comfortable inversion range.
subTechniques.dosage: 3–5 contractions of 5–10 seconds at low effort.
subTechniques.reassess: Inversion/eversion ROM, lateral-ankle comfort and single-leg stance.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: This is not a treatment for an acute unstable lateral ankle sprain; stability and healing stage come first.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid aggressive inversion when lateral-ligament injury is acute or unstable.
